slides.title:
Solar forecasting
with agent-assisted
experiments
slides.body:
Track forecasting experiments and evaluate changes to the training code.
A four-hour Python workshop using real satellite observations.
slides.notes: We’re going to use satellite observations to forecast X-ray flux thirty minutes ahead and solar images one hour ahead. We’ll start with persistence, train a few small models, and record enough information to compare their results. Once that comparison works, we’ll let an agent modify the training code and test whether its changes reduce forecast error. The small models and short training runs fit a CPU workshop; this is not an operational solar forecast.

slides.title: Prepare a forecast for the lab’s weekly review
slides.body:
Fictional lab · the principal investigator

“For this week’s review, bring a forecast we can reproduce.”

You’re the researcher.

Use two weeks of real satellite observations to make a forecast, measure its errors, and save enough information for a colleague to repeat it.

Start by testing whether the latest observation already makes a reasonable forecast.
slides.notes: Our fictional lab has a weekly forecast review. The principal investigator, or PI, wants a result the team can repeat. You are the researcher preparing it. The observations are real and come from February 2014. First we will check whether copying the current measurement predicts the future well enough to beat a trained model. This is a small teaching experiment, not a space-weather service.

slides.title: Two forecasts from real solar observations
slides.body:
Real training observations. NOAA GOES-15 and NASA/SDO AIA 171 Å; prepared with SunPy.

Measurements: use the previous hour to predict flux 30 minutes ahead.

Images: use two observations to predict an image one hour ahead.
slides.notes: Read the instruments before discussing models. The left plot measures solar X-ray flux; the right image records extreme-ultraviolet light at 171 Å. These are real February 2014 observations, prepared at a small scale for CPU teaching. The image uses false color. We are testing forecasts, not predicting a reliable flare warning.

Saving those records will also let us test code written by the research agent later.

slides.body:

slides.title: Predict X-ray flux 30 minutes ahead
slides.body: Predict log10 XRS-B flux. A forecast window includes observations, timestamps, and a future target.
slides.notes: Read the timeline from left to right. The model receives sixty minutes of X-ray flux measurements and predicts XRS-B thirty minutes after the last input. Flux is measured in watts per square metre. We take log10 because values span a wide range; the forecast error is therefore in log-flux units. The model never receives the future target as an input.

slides.title: Locate the observed history and future target
slides.body: The two lines are observations. The orange point is the future target; no model forecast is plotted.
slides.notes: Each input contains two channels and sixty one-minute samples, from minute minus fifty-nine through zero. Only XRS-B is predicted thirty minutes later. This plot reverses input standardization to show both channels in log-flux units. The target point is kept out of the input tensor.

slides.title: Use earlier dates to train, later dates to test
slides.body: February 2014, UTC. Fit normalization on training data only.
slides.notes: Train on February 1–10, choose models using February 11–12, and leave February 13–14 for the final comparison. Every input and the target of a window must belong to one partition. Fit normalization using training data only.

slides.title: Normalize the inputs without changing the target units
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="normalization" />
slides.notes: load_goes first takes log10 of both flux channels. It fits one mean and standard deviation per channel using training inputs only, then reuses those values for validation and final inputs. The target remains unstandardized log10 XRS-B. That is why persistence returns split["persistence"] rather than copying a standardized tensor entry.

slides.title: Leave out windows with missing observations
slides.body: <SolarDataRules mode="gaps" />
slides.notes: February 8 is absent from the prepared GOES source archive. A window that needs those readings cannot be used. Filling the absence with zero would tell the model that the instrument measured zero flux, which it did not.

slides.title: Start by copying the latest reading
slides.body:
```python def persistence_forecast(split): # Latest observed value becomes the future prediction. ... ```

Predict flux 30 minutes ahead by copying the latest reading.

This uses only a reading we already have. It does not look at the future target.
Input: The latest observed reading in each windowOutput: One 30-minute-ahead prediction per window
slides.notes: Persistence means predicting that the latest value will stay the same. Solar observations are correlated over time, so this simple baseline can be hard to beat. At the lab review, someone will ask why we needed a neural network if copying the last reading worked. We should run that comparison before they ask.

slides.title: Measure how far the prediction missed
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="error" />
slides.notes: For each forecast, subtract the observed log-flux target, take the absolute error, then average across windows. Lower is better. The average can hide a bad interval, so we also inspect the curves. Keep flux error separate from the later image score.

slides.body:
```python with session.stage( "measurement/run", config=config, sources={"candidate.py": source}, inputs={"dataset": dataset_version, "split": "validation"}, ) as stage: if stage.needs_run: result = train_model(data, config) stage.record(result) ```

slides.title: What changes during one training step
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="training" />
slides.notes: In fit, the GOES model predicts a batch and computes squared error against training targets. The shared loss function has an all-ones mask for GOES; the image exercise later uses the mask to select disk pixels. loss.backward computes gradients. Adam updates the forecasting model weights. The training targets participate in these updates. Validation inputs are predicted without gradients, and validation targets are scored by the parent process outside candidate code.

slides.title: Restore a completed run after a restart
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="checkpoint" />
slides.notes: The local completion record tells the notebook which work finished. The checkpoint Artifact stores a copy in your project. If the runtime is replaced, restore the checkpoint before continuing. An upload failure can be retried using the local files.

slides.title: Changing settings, choosing models, and editing code
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="search" />
slides.notes: There are three different operations here. Hyperparameter search supplies different values to the same implementation, such as learning rate or width. Architecture comparison chooses between implementations we already wrote, such as an MLP and a temporal CNN. Later, the research agent will write a code change that our current configuration options cannot express, such as replacing squared training loss with absolute loss. We’ll test that changed program with the same dates and scoring rule.

slides.title: How the MLP uses an hour of measurements
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="mlp" />
slides.notes: The actual candidate code flattens a two-by-sixty input into one hundred twenty values. A linear layer learns weights for every input position, followed by ReLU and a linear scalar output. Width is sixteen or thirty-two in the search. The diagram omits the batch dimension and draws a few hidden units to represent the layer.

slides.title: How the temporal CNN uses the same measurements
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="cnn" />
slides.notes: The same two-by-sixty input now passes through a five-sample convolution with padding two. Filter weights are reused along time. The output has width channels and sixty positions; AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) averages over time, then the linear layer predicts one value. This compares two implemented computations, not just two model names.

slides.body:

Small MLP16, 32, 16.001, .001, .00360 steps each
Temporal CNN16, 32, 16.001, .001, .00360 steps each
Seed 17. Batch size 32. The notebook records the active values.
slides.notes: The MLP reads the history as a fixed set of inputs. The temporal CNN applies shared filters along time. We’ll try three settings for each: widths sixteen and thirty-two, and learning rates .001 and .003. Every run gets seed seventeen, batch size thirty-two, and sixty training steps. That small budget keeps the exercise short; it does not establish which architecture would win after longer training.

slides.title: Predict the solar image one hour ahead
slides.body: AIA 171 Å. Prepared 64 × 64 arrays. One-hour forecasting.
slides.notes: Now we give the model images from sixty minutes ago and now, and ask for the image sixty minutes ahead. The AIA 171 Å arrays are 64 by 64 pixels so the exercise can run on CPU.

slides.title: Track the image model with the same experiment records
slides.body: The input and prediction changed shape. Source, settings, weights, and evidence still belong together. The image score uses normalized log1p intensity.
slides.notes: The inputs are now images, but we still save the same kinds of records: data, code, settings, weights, and predictions. Image values use normalized log1p intensity, so their errors have a different scale from the GOES errors.

slides.title: See exactly which images become input and target
slides.body:
First accepted training window. All three images share the same intensity scale.
The target is hidden from the model during prediction. It is used afterward to measure the miss.
slides.notes: Read the observation times. Channel zero is the earlier image; channel one is the current image. The third image is the future target. These are three real observations from a training window, not three outputs of an AI image generator.

slides.title: Predicting the future image with a small CNN
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="residual" :reveal="1" />
slides.notes: The two observations become two input channels. The CNN returns one channel containing its predicted future image. The batch dimension stays the same: input shape is batch by two by sixty-four by sixty-four, and output shape is batch by one by sixty-four by sixty-four. This direct predictor has to produce the whole image from its learned weights.

slides.title: Predict a correction to the current image
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="residual" :reveal="2" />
slides.notes: Much of the current image may remain similar one hour later. We can copy that image and ask the network to predict the correction. Add the network output to x[:, 1:2], the current-image channel. The slice preserves the channel dimension. If the correction is zero, the model returns persistence exactly. The local check will test that behavior.

slides.title: Implement the residual predictor’s forward pass
slides.body:
```python def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) # [batch, 1, 64, 64] current_image = x[:, 1:2] # keep the channel axis return current_image + correction ```
Input: earlier image + current imageOutput: one future image per example

Check: if correction is zero, the forecast equals the current image.
slides.notes: The diagram and code describe the same addition. Ask participants why x[:, 1] would remove a dimension and why x[:, 1:2] preserves it. The notebook implementation also branches on architecture so the convolutional comparison still returns only the network output.

slides.title: Inspect the correction produced by the saved model
slides.body: First validation case. Current image and forecast use the same intensity scale; the middle panel shows a signed correction.
slides.notes: The center image is calculated from the saved manual residual forecast minus the current input. It shows what this trained network added. It is not the physical change observed on the Sun. Zero is white in the correction view, with negative and positive values on opposite sides of the colorbar. The panels show the equation implemented by forward.

slides.title: Measure prediction error inside the solar disk
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="mask" />
slides.notes: This is a diagram of the scoring calculation, not a forecast. The fixed mask assigns one to disk pixels and zero outside. Multiply absolute errors by the mask, average over the selected pixels per image, then average images. A changed off-disk pixel must not affect the score.

slides.title: Check the image scorer on three known errors
slides.body:
```python absolute_error = np.abs(prediction - target) per_image = (absolute_error * disk_mask).sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```
Identical arrays: score 0Every disk pixel +1: score 1Only off-disk pixels +1: score 0
slides.notes: Run the three local examples before training. They explain what the scorer measures. The participant writes this development scorer, and the protected primary scorer checks the comparison with the same published rule. Missing or invalid predictions are not zero error.

slides.title: Training loss and evaluation error have different jobs
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="loss" />
slides.notes: The training loss supplies gradients for the optimizer. The evaluation metric scores the finished predictions. Our starting loss uses squared error, while the comparison uses absolute error inside the disk. A candidate can change the loss to alter how weights are learned. We keep the evaluation metric fixed so we can compare the resulting forecasts.

slides.title: Which model is being trained?
slides.body: <SolarMechanism mode="weights" />
slides.notes: The language model and the forecasting network have different roles. GLM writes Python using its fixed pretrained weights; we are not fine-tuning it. The small forecasting network trains new weights each time we test candidate Python. We send its validation results back to the language model when requesting the next edit.

slides.title: Ask for two changes to the same starting code
slides.body: Harness²-inspired: our probes train forecasting weights and include validation scores.
slides.notes: Both candidates start from the same source and training configuration. We ask the agent to explain each proposed change, then review its diff. This uses the Propose–Probe–Compose structure from Harness². In our teaching adaptation, a probe trains forecasting weights and gives validation results to the editor. It differs from the paper’s task protocol.

slides.title: The first proposal changes one loss operation
slides.body:
```python def training_loss(prediction, target, mask): # Before: square each miss. # After: take its absolute size. return ((prediction - target).abs() * mask).sum() / mask.sum() ```
− (prediction - target).square()
+ (prediction - target).abs()

Agent’s hypothesis: training on absolute error may help the fixed absolute-error score. The probe tests that claim.
slides.notes: This is the actual first-round Candidate A edit in v0.3.0. It changes the training objective, while the evaluation scorer remains fixed. The alternative candidate retains the original squared loss. The diff establishes the proposed change; it does not establish an improvement until both run.

slides.title: Train and score each candidate
slides.body: Use the same training and validation data. Keep failed runs visible.
slides.notes: Train each candidate on the same training dates and compare its validation error. If one fails before producing a forecast, inspect the error and leave its score missing.

slides.title: Choose or combine changes using the probe results
slides.body: The agent can keep A, keep B, combine changes, or retain the starting code.
slides.notes: After both probes, the agent receives their code and validation results. It can keep one candidate, combine changes, or retain the starting source. Two suggestions do not obligate the lab to accept two changes. Read its rationale beside the scores. The dashed lines show which results it reviewed; they do not mean both candidates were merged into the selected code.

slides.title: Train the composed version before adopting it
slides.body: Run the selected code on the same training and validation dates.
slides.notes: A combined edit has not yet been measured, so it needs its own training run. Even if the agent retains an existing version, the controller tests the chosen source and records the result. This separates the decision about what to keep from the execution that confirms what ran.

slides.title: Adopt the tested code only if validation error is lower
slides.body: <SolarDataRules mode="adoption" />
slides.notes: The composition is a proposed source version. After it trains, choose_adoption compares its fixed validation_error with the parent. A strictly lower score adopts the tested version. Equal error, a higher error, or failed execution retains the parent. The decision and the execution are separate records. This rule uses no final-test score.

slides.title: Open the training call behind the chosen version
slides.body:
Check the configuration, then find validation_error in the returned result.Open the selected training call ↗
Recorded v0.3.0 round 2 composition test. “error” is forecast error here, not an exception.
slides.notes: The operation trained and validated the selected source. Find the returned score and compare the run to the saved source artifact. An error metric of 0.110916 is the forecasting metric, not a tool failure. If a span actually failed, inspect its exception separately.

slides.title: Use the selected code and results in round two
slides.body: Use the selected code and what the first tests showed to plan the next changes.
slides.notes: Round two begins with the code selected in round one and a saved lesson explaining what the probes showed. The agent reads both before proposing its next edits. It may now change code introduced by its previous proposal. That repeated use of the earlier result is the recursive part of this research procedure.

slides.title: Propose and test two changes
slides.body:
Inspect next_research_action in 6. Test agent-written changes to the image model.
  1. Propose two code changes. Read both diffs.
  2. Confirm review of Candidate A → Test Candidate A. Confirm review of Candidate B → Test Candidate B.
  3. Record my comparison, then Request a composition.
Check your work: Each candidate’s proposal diff and training result are linked in Agent Lens.
slides.notes: Keep this slide visible while participants propose and test the first two candidates. Ask them to explain each diff before confirming review. After both tests, record a comparison and request the agent’s choice.

slides.title: Test the selected code, then begin round two
slides.body:
Continue the same workbench.
  1. Confirm review of composition, then Test the composition.
  2. Click Save the adopted version and lesson. Check whether the parent was retained.
  3. Repeat the process in round two using the previous outcome.
Check your work: Open the selected version from each round and explain why it was kept.
slides.notes: Give participants fifteen minutes for the tested selection and the second round. Retaining the previous code is a valid outcome. Ask why it was retained, then show its saved execution rather than treating KEEP as skipped work.

This deck diagram explains the process. The notebook’s branch view links the participant’s own files, decisions, traces, and results.

slides.title: Keep the selected code and weights fixed for final evaluation
slides.body: <SolarComputation mode="inference" />
slides.notes: We have used validation dates to choose the version we will bring to the review. Save that source and its trained weights together before looking at February thirteenth and fourteenth. Final evaluation loads those weights and predicts the reserved inputs without training or selecting again. If we edit after inspecting these results, we need new reserved dates to test the next claim.

slides.title: Load the saved weights to make final predictions
slides.body:
```python model = build_model(input_shape, frozen_config) model.load_state_dict(saved_weights) model.eval() with torch.no_grad(): prediction = model(final_inputs) ```
There is no optimizer step in this stage.
slides.notes: Load the saved weights, switch to evaluation mode, and predict without an optimizer step. Final evaluation measures the selected trained model; it does not train another one.

slides.title: Put the attribute inside the tool scope
slides.body:
```python
def instrument_tool(observation):
    with tracing.Tool(
        name=observation["name"],
        arguments=observation["arguments"],
        result=observation["result"],
        started_at=stamp(observation["started_at"]),
        ended_at=stamp(observation["ended_at"]),
    ) as tool:
        tool.set_attributes({"workshop.exercise": "solar-research"})
        if observation.get("error"):
            tool.record_error(RuntimeError(observation["error"]))
```
slides.notes: The attribute is attached inside the Tool scope. The complete notebook function also supplies its call identity and outer conversation. Use the operation’s timestamps so Agent Lens shows when the work happened, not when it was uploaded.

slides.title: Return a copy of the latest observation
slides.notes: The prepared split includes the last observed reading for each forecast window. Return a copy so later changes to the prediction array cannot alter the dataset.

slides.title: Implement the training loss and forecast metric
slides.notes: Subtract prediction and target, take absolute values, and average. A prediction of one against a target of zero gives one. These are log10 flux units. The training loss above it is separate and uses squared error.

slides.title: Compare the settings and loss curves
slides.body:
Open two runs from the Sweep. Compare their model, width, learning rate, and training steps.

Then open the loss curves. A lower validation error is easier to interpret when you can see how each model trained.

If a run failed, inspect its error. A missing score cannot rank that model.
slides.notes: Open the configuration and curve for two runs. Find the settings they share and the value that differs. If training failed, inspect the error rather than assigning a score to a forecast that does not exist.

slides.title: Average the error inside the disk mask
slides.body:
```python def my_image_mae(prediction, target, disk_mask): errors = np.abs(prediction - target) * disk_mask per_image = errors.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) per_image /= disk_mask.sum(axis=(1, 2, 3)) return float(per_image.mean()) ```

Test zero error, constant +1 error, and an error only outside the mask.
slides.notes: The mask selects the solar disk. Compute the sum and count per image, then average across images. Check identical arrays, a constant one-unit difference, and a difference only outside the mask.

slides.title: Add the correction to input channel 1
slides.body:
```python def forward(self, x): correction = self.net(x) if architecture == "residual": return x[:, 1:2] + correction return correction ```
The current image is input channel 1. The return has one channel.
slides.notes: Channel zero is the earlier image and channel one is the current image. Add the correction to channel one. With a zero correction, this function returns the current image exactly.

slides.title: Return validation evidence only
slides.notes: First check that the record belongs to validation. Then return only the listed evidence fields. The current source is supplied separately. The final-test example should raise an error before the agent sees it.

slides.body:
```python candidate = proposal["candidates"][candidate_index] probe = run_training( session, stage_name, candidate["source"], image_splits, parent["config"], dataset_version, metric_source, ) ```
Use the candidate’s source here. Passing the parent would train the old program again.
slides.notes: Pass candidate['source'] to training, along with the shared configuration. Passing the parent source here would train the old program while the interface appeared to test a new proposal. Open the saved candidate.py if the result looks suspicious.

slides.body:
Load each selected model’s saved weights and predict the reserved dates.

Compare the three image forecasts at one timestamp. The input images and observed future should match across all three rows.

Persistence copies the current image and needs no trained weights.
slides.notes: The selected weights are already trained. Load them and predict the final inputs. Compare the same target timestamps across all versions; persistence uses the current image directly.

slides.body:

Starting residual model0.122116
A · use absolute training loss0.120553
B · retain squared training loss0.122116

The composition selected A. Its separate test reproduced 0.120553.

slides.title: Round 2: start the correction at zero
slides.body:
```python if architecture == 'residual': nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].weight) nn.init.zeros_(self.net[-1].bias) # The residual forward pass remains: return prediction + x[:, 1:2] ```
The round-one absolute loss stays. Zero initial correction makes the initial forecast persistence.
slides.notes: This is the second-round selected edit in v0.3.0. The last convolution starts at zero; before training, the residual correction is zero. The model begins at persistence and learns a correction. Its probe and separate composition test produce the measured validation score.

slides.title: Zero initialization applies only to the output layer
slides.body: <SolarDataRules mode="zero-head" />
slides.notes: The recorded second-round edit zeros the weights and bias of self.net[-1], the last Conv2d. Earlier convolution layers retain their normal initialization. The last layer initially returns zero, so adding its output to the current image reproduces persistence before training. Adam can then learn a correction. This explains the edit; its measured effect is still limited to the recorded comparison.

slides.title: Round 2: sampling without replacement did not reduce error
slides.body:
Tested sourceValidation error ↓
Starting absolute-loss model0.120553
A · zero-initialize the residual head0.110916
B · sample without replacement0.120557

The composition selected A. It did not combine the unhelpful sampling change.

Keep the tested sampling result alongside the selected version for comparison.
slides.notes: Candidate B changes the batch sampling to seeded permutations. Its validation error is essentially the same as the parent and slightly higher. The composition keeps zero initialization and rejects the sampling change. Do not attribute a benefit to an untested combination.
